planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full to part sun; this Walters Gardens Rainbow Rhythm tetraploid builds a vigorous clump within a couple of seasons.

directions: A Rainbow Rhythm introduction from Walters Gardens, this tetraploid daylily opens coral-pink flowers about five and a half inches across with a rich cranberry-red eye zone and a soft yellow-trimmed edge on wide, piecrust-ruffled petals. Scapes reach roughly two feet tall and carry fragrant blooms in early midseason, with a dependable second flush later in the year. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom counts high.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this semi-evergreen tetraploid daylily reblooms once established.

directions: Creamy to ivory-yellow flowers with a prominent wine-purple eye and a matching picotee edge along attractively ruffled petals distinguish this Walters Gardens introduction, which earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 2001. The semi-evergreen tetraploid foliage supports scapes about two feet tall that open their first flush in early midseason and rebloom later in the summer. Divide clumps every few years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this evergreen tetraploid daylily tends to run shorter in the garden than its registered height.

directions: Born to Run carries rich rosy-red flowers edged in a heavily ruffled, creamy-yellow picotee band, with a narrow pale-pink watermark hovering above a lime-green throat. Registered around 28 inches tall, growers commonly see shorter 20-to-22-inch scapes in the garden, blooming and reblooming through midsummer on evergreen tetraploid foliage. Divide clumps every few years in spring to keep the planting floriferous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full to part sun; this fragrant tetraploid daylily holds its deep color without fading.

directions: This Walters Gardens tetraploid daylily produces wine-purple flowers rimmed with a heavily ruffled, crisp lemon-yellow picotee edge above a yellow-and-purple eye zone, with color that resists fading in summer heat. Scapes stand roughly two feet tall and carry fragrant blooms in midseason, followed by a second flush later on. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring for best performance.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this tall reblooming tetraploid tolerates poor soil and roadside salt exposure well.

directions: Hybridized in 1996 and awarded an AHS Honorable Mention in 2003, Desert Flame sends up scapes carrying large, flaming red-orange flowers around five and a half inches across, ruffled and recurved with a lime-green throat and contrasting orange stamens. It opens its first round of bloom in midseason and reliably reblooms again in fall. This tough tetraploid tolerates lean soil and urban stress, and benefits from division every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; well-branched, heavily budded scapes hold flowers flat and open for most of the day.

directions: Erin Lea opens broad, rounded, sunny golden-yellow self flowers edged in frilly, fringed ruffles, with petals that open flat so the five-and-a-half to six inch blooms read larger than their measured size. It earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 1998. Strong, well-branched scapes about two feet tall carry a heavy bud count through midseason. Divide clumps every few years in spring to keep the planting productive.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this fragrant, semi-evergreen tetraploid reblooms after its main midseason flush.

directions: Hybridized by Karol Emmerich and awarded an AHS Honorable Mention in 2011, Handwriting on the Wall blends soft peach petals that wash toward a wine-purple eye and a golden-yellow throat, each ruffled petal finished with a thin purple picotee edge, giving the flower a watercolor-like gradient. Scapes around two feet tall bear fragrant blooms on semi-evergreen tetraploid foliage, flowering in midseason with a dependable second flush. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain strong bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this early-blooming tetraploid carries its flowers on candelabra-branched scapes.

directions: Monterrey Jack bears light-yellow flowers of near-perfect form, defined by a well-marked raspberry-red eye, with broad rounded petals that open wide and flat to about five and a half inches across. Candelabra-branched scapes roughly two feet tall display the ruffled blooms starting early in the season, ahead of most other tetraploid daylilies. Divide clumps every few years in spring to keep flowering strong.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this fragrant tetraploid holds sunfast color through midsummer heat.

directions: Passion for Red produces very sunfast, vividly orange-red flowers six to seven inches across, with a contrasting yellow eye and throat zone visible across all six tepals. Fragrant blooms open in early midseason on tall scapes, with a partial rebloom later in summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the display vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; bred as an improvement on the older cultivar El Desperado, with better branching and higher bud count.

directions: Star of the North is distinguished by uniquely triangular, pale-yellow petals set off by a large wine-purple eye and a razor-thin matching picotee edge, with a faint fragrance that is unusual for a daylily. Walters Gardens describes it as an improvement on its older parent line, 'El Desperado,' with better branching and a higher bud count. Tall scapes around three feet carry the blooms in early July, with reliable rebloom. Divide clumps every few years in spring to sustain strong flowering.
